subject: Cardiovascular
subtopic: Left-to-right congenital shunts and Eisenmenger syndrome
vignette: A 3-week-old boy who fed and grew normally in the first days of life now tires and sweats during feeds. Examination reveals a harsh holosystolic murmur at the lower left sternal border. Echocardiography shows a defect in the interventricular septum, and an oxygen saturation step-up is measured in the right ventricle and pulmonary artery.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Atrial septal defect
Patent ductus arteriosus
Ventricular septal defect
Tricuspid atresia
Coarctation of the aorta

explanation_correct: A ventricular septal defect is the most common left-to-right shunt (frequency VSD > ASD > PDA). It is typically asymptomatic at birth and may manifest weeks later, when the fall in pulmonary vascular resistance allows left-to-right flow: left atrial and ventricular volume overload causes the feeding intolerance and diaphoresis, and the O2 saturation step-up in the RV and pulmonary artery confirms the shunt. Most smaller defects self-resolve; large untreated defects can raise pulmonary blood flow and cause Eisenmenger syndrome and heart failure.

explanation_incorrect.A: An ASD produces a systolic ejection murmur with a wide, fixed split S2, and the O2 step-up occurs in the RA, RV, and pulmonary artery, not a holosystolic murmur at the lower left sternal border.
explanation_incorrect.B: A PDA produces a continuous, machine-like murmur rather than a holosystolic murmur, and does not produce a saturation step-up in the RV or pulmonary artery.
explanation_incorrect.D: Tricuspid atresia is a right-to-left shunt with early cyanosis, absence of the tricuspid valve, a hypoplastic RV, and ECG findings of RA and LV hypertrophy.
explanation_incorrect.E: Coarctation of the aorta is not an intracardiac shunt; it causes upper-extremity hypertension with weak, delayed femoral pulses and no saturation step-up in the right heart.

educationalObjective: VSD is the most common left-to-right shunt, presents with a holosystolic murmur after a symptom-free period at birth, and shows an O2 saturation step-up in the RV and pulmonary artery.

subject: Cardiovascular
subtopic: Left-to-right congenital shunts and Eisenmenger syndrome
vignette: A 30-year-old woman is found to have a systolic ejection murmur at the upper left sternal border and a wide, fixed split S2. Echocardiography shows a defect in the interatrial septum with a left-to-right shunt and an O2 saturation step-up in the RA, RV, and pulmonary artery. She has no dysmorphic features and is otherwise asymptomatic.
question: Which of the following best characterizes this patient's most likely lesion?

options.text: Ostium secundum defect — the most common ASD and usually an isolated finding
Ostium primum defect — the most common ASD and usually an isolated finding
Patent foramen ovale — a true septal defect that usually requires surgical closure
Ventricular septal defect — the defect responsible for a wide, fixed split S2
Total anomalous pulmonary venous return — the most common cause of fixed splitting of S2

explanation_correct: An atrial septal defect with a systolic ejection murmur and a wide, fixed split S2 is most commonly an ostium secundum defect, which is usually an isolated finding. Ostium primum defects are rarer and usually occur with other cardiac anomalies (classically in Down syndrome). ASDs are associated with Down syndrome, and symptoms range from none to heart failure.

explanation_incorrect.B: Ostium primum defects are the rarer ASD type and typically occur with other cardiac anomalies rather than as isolated findings.
explanation_incorrect.C: A patent foramen ovale is due to failed fusion of the septum primum and secundum and is distinct from a true atrial septal defect; it is usually asymptomatic rather than a lesion requiring routine closure.
explanation_incorrect.D: A VSD produces a holosystolic murmur and an O2 step-up in the RV and pulmonary artery; the wide, fixed split S2 is characteristic of an ASD.
explanation_incorrect.E: TAPVR is a right-to-left (cyanotic) defect in which pulmonary veins drain into the right heart; it is not the lesion producing a wide, fixed split S2 here.

educationalObjective: Ostium secundum ASDs are the most common type, usually isolated, and produce a systolic ejection murmur with a wide, fixed split S2.

subject: Cardiovascular
subtopic: Left-to-right congenital shunts and Eisenmenger syndrome
vignette: A 26-year-old woman with a known asymptomatic atrial septal defect presents with acute left-sided weakness and slurred speech; imaging confirms a middle cerebral artery infarct. Her symptoms began while she was lifting weights at the gym. Transthoracic echo with bubble study shows bubbles crossing from the right atrium to the left atrium during the Valsalva release.
question: Which of the following best describes the mechanism of her stroke?

options.text: A thrombus formed in the left atrium embolized directly to the cerebral circulation
Chronic volume overload caused pulmonary arterial hypertension with permanent shunt reversal (Eisenmenger syndrome)
A venous thrombus bypassed the lungs by crossing the ASD during a transient right-to-left shunt, becoming a systemic arterial embolus
The Valsalva maneuver induced an O2 saturation step-up in the RA, RV, and pulmonary artery that thrombosed the shunt
An embolus from a carotid artery atherosclerotic plaque lodged in the middle cerebral artery

explanation_correct: This is a paradoxical embolism: systemic venous thrombi can use an ASD to bypass the lungs and become systemic arterial emboli during a temporary shunt reversal, which occurs with transient increases in right-sided pressures such as lifting weights (or straining with Valsalva) or in established Eisenmenger syndrome. The bubble study crossing during Valsalva release confirms the transient right-to-left passage.

explanation_incorrect.A: Paradoxical emboli arise from the systemic venous circulation, not from the left atrium; a left atrial source would not require the ASD at all.
explanation_incorrect.B: Eisenmenger syndrome is one setting in which shunt reversal and paradoxical emboli occur, but this patient had a transient reversal during weight lifting rather than established Eisenmenger physiology.
explanation_incorrect.D: An O2 saturation step-up in the RA, RV, and pulmonary artery reflects the usual baseline left-to-right shunting across an ASD and does not cause thrombosis of the defect.
explanation_incorrect.E: Carotid atherosclerotic disease is an unlikely stroke mechanism in a 26-year-old with a known ASD and symptoms triggered by weight lifting.

educationalObjective: ASDs can permit paradoxical emboli when a transient shunt reversal (weight lifting, Valsalva, Eisenmenger syndrome) lets venous thrombi bypass the lungs.

subject: Cardiovascular
subtopic: Left-to-right congenital shunts and Eisenmenger syndrome
vignette: A premature newborn has a continuous, 'machine-like' murmur at the left infraclavicular area, a wide pulse pressure, and bounding peripheral pulses. Echocardiography shows a patent ductus arteriosus with left-to-right flow.
question: Which of the following factors maintain the patency of this patient's shunt?

options.text: Decreased prostaglandin synthesis and high oxygen tension
Prostaglandin E synthesis and low oxygen tension
Increased oxygen tension and decreased prostaglandin synthesis
Bradykinin release and elevated arterial oxygen content
Increased pulmonary vascular resistance after the first breath

explanation_correct: Patency of the ductus arteriosus is maintained by prostaglandin E (PGE) synthesis and low oxygen tension. In the fetal period the shunt is right to left (normal); after birth, the drop in pulmonary vascular resistance converts it to a left-to-right shunt that produces the continuous machine-like murmur and can lead to progressive RVH and/or LVH and heart failure.

explanation_incorrect.A: Decreased PGE synthesis and high oxygen tension are conditions that promote ductal closure, not patency.
explanation_incorrect.C: This combination describes the postnatal conditions that close the ductus; it is the opposite of what maintains patency.
explanation_incorrect.D: Bradykinin and elevated oxygen are associated with postnatal ductal constriction and closure, not maintenance of patency.
explanation_incorrect.E: Increased pulmonary vascular resistance is the fetal state that drives the normal right-to-left shunt through the ductus; after birth its fall converts the shunt to left-to-right but does not itself keep the ductus open.

educationalObjective: The ductus arteriosus is held open by PGE synthesis and low O2 tension; a persistent PDA produces a continuous machine-like murmur.

subject: Cardiovascular
subtopic: Left-to-right congenital shunts and Eisenmenger syndrome
vignette: A medical student is reviewing the neonatal transition of ductal flow in a newborn whose ductus arteriosus fails to close. In utero, the ductal shunt was right to left (normal). Over the first days of life, the direction of flow through the patent ductus reverses.
question: Which of the following hemodynamic changes converts the fetal right-to-left ductal shunt into a left-to-right shunt after birth?

options.text: Increase in pulmonary vascular resistance at delivery
Functional closure of the foramen ovale
Decrease in systemic vascular resistance
Decrease in pulmonary vascular resistance with the first breaths
Progressive right ventricular hypertrophy raising right ventricular systolic pressure

explanation_correct: In the neonatal period, the fall in pulmonary vascular resistance with the first breaths lowers pulmonary artery pressure below systemic pressure, so the shunt through a patent ductus arteriosus becomes left to right. This left-to-right flow causes progressive RVH and/or LVH and eventually heart failure, and an uncorrected PDA can later produce differential cyanosis of the lower extremities.

explanation_incorrect.A: An increase in pulmonary vascular resistance would maintain or worsen right-to-left (fetal-type) flow through the ductus; the neonatal fall in resistance is what reverses the direction.
explanation_incorrect.B: Foramen ovale closure is part of the normal transition but does not determine the direction of flow across the ductus arteriosus.
explanation_incorrect.C: The critical change is the drop in pulmonary vascular resistance; a fall in systemic vascular resistance would actually favor right-to-left flow.
explanation_incorrect.E: Progressive RVH is a later consequence of the left-to-right shunt and volume/pressure load, not the change that establishes the left-to-right direction.

educationalObjective: After birth, the fall in pulmonary vascular resistance converts the normal fetal right-to-left ductal shunt into a left-to-right shunt in a PDA.

subject: Cardiovascular
subtopic: Left-to-right congenital shunts and Eisenmenger syndrome
vignette: A 34-year-old man with a heart murmur since infancy that was never treated now has exertional dyspnea, central cyanosis, and finger clubbing. Laboratory studies show hemoglobin 21 g/dL (polycythemia). Echocardiography shows right ventricular hypertrophy and reversal of a chronic ventricular-level shunt, with blood now flowing from right to left.
question: Which of the following sequences best explains this patient's current condition?

options.text: Uncorrected left-to-right shunt → increased pulmonary blood flow → pathologic vascular remodeling → pulmonary arterial hypertension → RVH → shunt reversal when RV pressure exceeds LV pressure
Anterosuperior displacement of the infundibular septum → right ventricular outflow obstruction → right-to-left flow across a VSD from birth
Idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension → right ventricular failure → acquisition of a new ventricular septal defect with right-to-left flow
Postnatal fall in pulmonary vascular resistance → left-to-right ductal flow → continuous murmur → differential cyanosis of the lower extremities only
Chronic right-to-left shunting from birth → polycythemia → hyperviscosity → secondary pulmonary arterial hypertension and clubbing

explanation_correct: This is Eisenmenger syndrome: an uncorrected left-to-right shunt (VSD, ASD, or PDA) increases pulmonary blood flow, causing pathologic remodeling of the pulmonary vasculature and pulmonary arterial hypertension. RVH develops to compensate, and the shunt reverses to right-to-left when RV pressure exceeds LV pressure, producing late cyanosis, clubbing, and polycythemia. The age of onset varies with the size and severity of the initial left-to-right shunt.

explanation_incorrect.B: This sequence describes tetralogy of Fallot, in which cyanosis is present early ('early cyanosis') because the right-to-left shunt is the primary defect, not a late consequence of an untreated left-to-right shunt.
explanation_incorrect.C: Eisenmenger syndrome is secondary to a congenital left-to-right shunt; primary pulmonary hypertension does not create a ventricular septal defect.
explanation_incorrect.D: This describes the physiology of an uncorrected PDA; its late differential cyanosis is confined to the lower extremities, whereas this patient has central cyanosis, clubbing, and polycythemia from a reversed VSD.
explanation_incorrect.E: In Eisenmenger syndrome, the pulmonary hypertension comes first from vascular remodeling due to the original left-to-right shunt, and the right-to-left shunting and polycythemia are secondary, not the initiating events.

educationalObjective: Eisenmenger syndrome is late cyanosis, clubbing, and polycythemia after an uncorrected left-to-right shunt causes pulmonary vascular remodeling, pulmonary hypertension, RVH, and shunt reversal.
